youtube_title: Why Your Cruise Between U.S. Ports Stops in Another Country 🦝⚖️
caption: Under the Passenger Vessel Services Act regulations, a non-U.S.-qualified ship can sail a round trip from one U.S. port with a nearby foreign stop — but ending at a different U.S. port needs a distant foreign port.
script: That random foreign stop on your cruise? It's there because of a law from eighteen eighty six. [disclaimer] Meet Gary. Gary books a cruise from Florida, around the Caribbean, and back. On day three, the ship stops in a random little foreign port. For four hours. Gary asks why. Nobody on board seems to know. It's a law called the Passenger Vessel Services Act. It limits foreign ships, like most big cruise ships, from carrying passengers from one American port to another. If a foreign ship only visits American ports, and you get off at a different American port, that breaks the rule. Wait. So the stop is about the law, not the beach? You see, it's like a game where you have to touch the wall before you come back. A quick stop nearby, then back to the same port you started at, and that's okay. But ending at a different American port needs a stop somewhere far away. There are special cases, like Puerto Rico. And this is the passenger rule, not the Jones Act for cargo. So the ship stops, the passengers buy a T shirt, and everyone gets back on. So the most important stop on Gary's cruise is the one he didn't even want. script_old: Why would a cruise between American ports bother stopping in another country? Sometimes, the law explains it. This is the Passenger Vessel Services Act, a U.S. law that limits carrying passengers between U.S. ports on ships that aren't qualified for that domestic trade, like foreign-flagged cruise ships. Customs regulations spell out how it works. If a cruise only visits U.S. ports, and passengers get off at a U.S. port, that's a violation. Now add a nearby foreign port, like one in Canada, Mexico, the Bahamas or the Caribbean. If passengers end the trip back at the same U.S. port where they boarded, the regulations don't treat that as a violation. That's one reason round-trip cruises often include a quick foreign stop. But if passengers end the trip at a different U.S. port, a nearby foreign stop isn't enough. The ship would need to visit a distant foreign port, one outside that nearby list. There are special cases too, like Puerto Rico. Here's the limit. A foreign stop doesn't make every itinerary legal, and this is the passenger rule, not the Jones Act rules for cargo. Cruise lines can ask Customs for an advisory ruling, and nothing here means any particular route is approved. [loop] So the next time your cruise makes a surprise stop abroad, remember
